81.content:
Introduction

This report summarises the key findings from the 2026 State of the Park Report update. Each of the twelve key features of the Peak District National Park are outlined below, assessing their distribution, condition, and key hazards they are at risk from. The current ‘state’ (condition) and the trend of this condition are given a rating, with an additional rating for the certainty of this assessment – the scales of these assessments are outlined below.

State

Trend

Certainty

Good condition

Improving

High

Moderate concern

No change

Moderate

Significant concern

Declining

Low

The certainty ratings for many features are low due to the scarcity of condition data available across features. For landscape and cultural heritage features, designated features for which there are more frequent condition assessments are used as a proxy. However, these features only represent a small proportion of the overall feature present in the National Park, and even for designated features where condition assessment should take place regularly, this information can often be upwards to 15 years old. Therefore, while this report offers a snapshot into the condition of the key features in the Peak District, ongoing assessment and monitoring of features will be needed to evaluate the success of actions which manage these features.

83.content:
Drivers of change

Each feature-assessment is accompanied by a ‘drivers of change’ diagram which summarises the key factors which have been assessed as likely to drive change to the feature, detailing some of the key hazards which is cause impacts to the feature. The size of the arrows in these diagrams indicates the level of risk from each driver.

72.content:
Woodland

State

Significant concern

Trend

Deteriorating

Certainty

Moderate

9.content:
Key findings

Total area: There are roughly 3,725ha of priority woodland habitats in the Peak District, which is 2.6% of the area of the National Park. Trees outside of woodlands make up the largest cumulative area of woodland habitats assessed in this report but by nature this is completely fragmented across the landscape in lone trees or small groups.

Distribution: These priority woodlands are highly fragmented and scattered across the National Park, and are unevenly distributed between and within the different Landscape Character Areas (LCAs). The most wooded areas LCA is the Derwent Valley, while in other areas woodland tend to be restricted to steep sided valleys and cloughs.

Condition: There are very limited data to assess the current condition of woodland habitat types; the limited condition records from Site of Special Scientific Interest monitoring suggest that where priority woodlands are within these protected sites, they are unlikely to be declining, however the scarcity of data makes the certainty of this very low.

Hazards:

  • Woodlands are being impacted by a range of factors that make it likely they are in deteriorating condition. Climate change is a key driver of change as it is changing the conditions which woodland habitats to survive, as well as increasing the likelihood of wildfire.
  • A key hazard for woodland in the Peak District is ash dieback disease, which has infected up to 99% of ash trees and as a result may cause the near complete loss of upland mixed ash woodlands.

73.content:
Grassland

State

Moderate concern

Trend

No change

Certainty

Low

45.content:
Key findings

Total area: There are around 14,156ha of priority grassland habitats in the Peak District with a further 10,161ha of good quality semi-improved grassland; this makes up around 17% of the area of the National Park.

Distribution: Grassland habitats are widely distributed across the National Park with different grassland types occurring locally within Landscape Character Areas as a result of underlying geology; calcareous grasslands in the limestone areas and acid grasslands in the gritstone areas. Purple moor grass and rush pasture occurs almost exclusively in the Southwest Peak, while good quality semi-improved grassland can be found across the National Park. 

Condition: Condition records are only available for grassland habitats within Sites of Special Scientific Interest which is only a sample of sites, and these records are often 10-20 years old which gives low certainty to an overall condition assessment. However, where records are available condition tends to be more likely to be favourable or improving than declining.

Hazards:

  • Land management decisions, particularly grazing, are a key factor putting pressure on grasslands, which rely on a balance of grazing to maintain their current state.
  • Climate change will also increasingly cause impact as pressures such as changes in rainfall and likelihood of wildfire increase.

74.content:
Freshwater & wetland

State Moderate concern Trend Improving Certainty Low

76.content:
Key findings

Total area: There is a total of 31,038ha of wetland habitats in the Peak District, 21% of the total area - with 3,065 ponds and 867km of rivers and streams making up the freshwater habitats. Blanket bog makes up 29,780km of the National Park, the largest signal area of any priority habitat type.

Distribution: Freshwater and wetland habitats are unevenly distributed across the National Park; the Dark Peak Landscape Character Area (LCA) is predominantly wetland with many rivers and streams, while the Eastern Moors and Southwest Peak have significant wetland areas. The White Peak LCA contains very few rivers due to the porous underlying limestone, while it does have the highest density of ponds, mostly associated with agricultural landscapes.

Condition: Wetland habitats within Sites of Special Scientific Interest have some limited condition data available, which generally indicates that they are in either favourable or recovering condition. Freshwater habitats rely on other sources for condition information, which generally indicate they are in a moderate condition. However, the certainty for this assessment is low due to the limited availability of condition data.

Hazards:

  • Climate change will be a primary driver of change in wetland and freshwater habitats as a result of changing precipitation and temperature patterns, effecting water availability which is vital to these habitats. Land management will have compound impacts as this can also impact drainage.
  • Pollution is also a more significant hazard in these habitats than others due to water transporting pollutants, which can become concentrated.

77.content:
Moorland & heath

Status Moderate concern Trend No change Certainty Low

79.content:
Key findings

Total area: There are around 20,658ha of priority moorland and heath habitat in the Peak District, with a further 4,919ha of grass moorland and fragmented heath which is important as it could be managed back into priority condition. This totals 18% of the National Park’s area.

Distribution: Moorland and heath is almost completely absent from the White Peak Landscape Character Area (LCA) but can be found extensively in the Dark Peak and Eastern Moors and in smaller fragments in the Southwest Peak and Derwent Valley. This shows these habitats predominate on the acidic soils primarily found in the areas with underlying gritstone geology.

Condition: No condition information is available for the non-priority moorland and heath habitats, so their condition is unknown. Upland and lowland heath, which are considered priority habitats, are considered to be in favourable or recovering condition where records are available, however confidence in these ratings is low.

Hazards:

  • A key hazard for moorland and heath habitats is uncontrolled fire, which can cause extensive damage and is becoming more likely as a result of climate change.
  • Changes in land management practices, for example away from grouse moor management, may also impact this habitat including it’s extent and species composition.

10.title: Introduction
10.description: Telling the story of the Peak District with data and evidence

11.content:
The Peak District National Park is Britain’s first national park, celebrating its 75th birthday in 2026. Taken as a whole, it is a treasured landscape that has been shaped and continues to evolve through the interaction of natural and cultural forces. It is a landscape of exceptional natural beauty that provides many benefits to people, from a sense of connection and identity to producing food and clean water, as well as being home to a wide variety of species and habitats.

This State of the Park Report draws on a wide range of technical information, research and local knowledge to provide an insight into the condition of the landscape through examining the different features that together make the landscape what it is. This report takes this evidence a step further, by presenting an assessment of the risks to these features as a result of factors which are driving change, from climate change to pollution to demographic and sociocultural change. This work will inform and support the Peak District National Park Management Plan, which will be reviewed and updated ready for a new plan to guide the work of all those who love and care for the National Park from 2028 to 2033.

How to use this report

This report has sections relating to the features of the National Park, and the factors that may impact them.

Use the menu on the left of the page to navigate between sections, while in-text links will guide you between related sections. Over time the report will grow and change as new data is released and our understanding of both the landscape and what is driving change within it evolves, so check back for the latest updates.

Wherever possible, data will relate to the area within the PDNP boundary and will draw from the latest evidence bases. However, this will not always be possible due to temporal and spatial constraints of the data and evidence available. Anyone with a special interest in a particular theme or data topic can request supporting technical information, or let us know about evidence we’re missing by contacting the Peak District National Park Authority using the email address strategy@peakdistrict.gov.uk.

11.title: Methodology
11.description: The Peak District National Park was designated because it exhibits a range of special qualities which are of national, and sometimes international, significance. This State of the Park Report assesses the condition of the constituent features of these special qualities, and which contribute toward the provision of the benefits of the National Park both within its boundaries and in its wider setting.

27.content:
How we will monitor the National Park

Effective policy making and evaluation is based on robust evidence. Evidence helps to guide decisions, from issues of national policy to choices about individual site management.

This State of the Park Report provides the evidence base from which to develop the National Park Management Plan by undertaking three steps:

  1. Assessing the condition of the key features of the National Park
  2. Identifying the key factors affecting these features
  3. Evaluating the level of risk posed by each of these factors to support the prioritisation of management actions to reduce their impact

In the process of developing the National Park Management Plan, the research and evidence gathered in this report will go on to support subsequent monitoring steps, including:

  1. Ensuring that appropriate long term data collection and monitoring mechanisms are in place to review management actions
  2. Collaborating with partners to develop and refine our evidence base over time

The methodology for how the first three of these steps were undertaken in this report is outlined below in more detail. If you have further questions or would like to collaborate to help develop our monitoring approach going forward, please contact strategy@peakdistrict.gov.uk.

28.content:
Definitions

This report uses a “feature and factor” based approach to understand landscape and landscape change. Key definitions that may be useful in engaging with this report are:

Feature

A tangible aspect of the landscape which, together with other features, constitutes the landscapes’ character, its special qualities and contributes towards the benefits it provides.

Factor

Something which is driving change to the features, positive or negative. May also be called “driver of change” or “pressure”.

Impact

The outcome of the interaction between the feature and the factor, i.e. how the features has changed.

Cause

The mechanism through which the factor has an impact on the feature, may otherwise be referred to as a hazard.

30.content:
Step 1- Feature condition assessment

Defining the features to be assessed

This report uses a list of features compiled from previous work for the Climate Change Vulnerability Assessment. These features were further consolidated and refined to align to the latest policy, for example using Protected Landscape Targets and Outcomes Framework priority habitats, and through discussion with expert officers within the Peak District National Park Authority.

Features were grouped with others with shared characteristics that as a result are likely to experience similar impacts, and therefore require similar management actions. This resulted in 3 feature families, 12 feature groups and 51 features.

32.content:
Condition evidence gathering

Evidence to assess the condition of the identified features was gathered through desk-based research between December 2025 and July 2026. This sought to answer three key questions regarding each feature:

  • Where is it?
  • How much is there?
  • What condition is it in?

Evidence to answer these questions was drawn from a variety of sources including data from relevant governmental departments, internal Peak District National Park Authority data, academic research and grey literature. Original analyses of data were undertaken where necessary.

 In many cases, evidence was limited to answering the first and second questions, with limited evidence to contribute to condition understanding for many features. Data gaps are identified on feature-group pages.

33.content:
Step 2 – Factor identification

A preliminary list of factors impacting the Peak District list was drawn up during previous work which defined the special qualities of the National Park. This was cross-referenced with the IPBES’s Global assessment report on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services[69] classification of direct and indirect drivers.

This led to a factor list which was tailored to the Peak District as a cultural landscape within its context, which also aligns with international best practice.

properties.caption: Direct and indirect drivers of change to ecosystems from IPBES’ Global assessment report on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services report.

36.content:
Step 3 – Risk assessment

The risk assessment methodology is drawn from Natural England’s State of Natural Capital Report and the Peak District National Park Authority’s Climate Change Vulnerability Assessment. It was determined that assessing risk at the level of the feature-group was most appropriate due to the availability of information and as this is a landscape-scale report having a higher resolution of assessment for risk is most appropriate.

Risk was estimated by:

  1. Determining what factors may cause impact to features over the next 5-10 years (including whether this impact is currently underway or whether it will continue beyond this period).
  2. Assigning a severity and impact rating for each factor against each feature-group based on how many impacts it is likely to cause, the consequences of these impacts, and the certainty and evidence availability that these are likely to occur.

Definitions of severity and impact used in this assessment:

Severity: A measure of how significant the impact will be on the feature which can include how and to what degree it will change the feature, how noticeable this would be to a specialist or non-specialist, the scale of the impact and how manageable the impact could be.

Likelihood: The chance or possibility that the impact will occur over the next five to ten years taking account of the availability and quality of projections, expert opinions and an estimation of the degree of change that will occur over this time period.

38.content:
The character of the landscape

Taken as a whole, the Peak District is a distinctive and treasured national landscape, while at a local scale there are many individual landscape types, each valued for their unique characteristics. This wide variety of landscapes include broad open moorlands, intimate enclosed farmlands, and wooded river valleys. These landscapes have been shaped by variations in geology and landform, ecological change, and a long history of settlement and use by people. Today's landscapes have a rich diversity of natural and cultural heritage, enjoyed today by local communities and visitors.

Understanding the characteristics of the different parts of the National Park is important to assess how they may be at risk from different factors or require different management. To do so, this report uses the Landscape Character Area (LCA) classification which was carried out for the Landscape Strategy 2009 by the Peak District National Park Authority.

40.content: While together these LCAs make up the Peak District landscape as a whole, they each have distinct characteristics which can be seen today in the types of land cover across the National Park. The topography and altitude of the Peak District has a significant bearing upon some types of land cover, whilst the climate will also affect the extent of certain vegetation types. Using the most recent UKCEH (the UK Centre for Ecology and Hydrology) land cover data from 2024, the different land cover types within different LCAs become visible; the Dark Peak dominated by bog, the Eastern Moors by acid grassland, and the White Peak by improved and calcareous grassland, for example.

42.content:
Legal status

The Peak District was designated as a National Park in 1951, giving it the statutory purposes to:

  • To conserve and enhance the natural beauty, wildlife and cultural heritage
  • To promote opportunities for the public understanding and enjoyment of the special qualities of the Parks

And a duty to:

  • To seek to foster the social and economic wellbeing of the local communities within the National Park in pursuit of our purposes.

In cases where an irreconcilable conflict exists between the two purposes, the first purpose should take precedence – this is known as the Sandford Principle.

Other key pieces of legislation and policy have an influence over the National Park, for example the National Planning Policy Framework which guides the work of the Peak District National Park as a Planning Authority, the Protected Landscapes Targets and Outcomes Framework guides the direction of land management in the National Park, and the Countryside and Rights of Way Act 2000 designates large parts of the National Park as open access for some recreational activities.

Governance and land ownership

There is no one person or organisation who is responsible for delivering these purposes for the landscape. The Peak District National Park Authority exists to guide this work and collaborate with stakeholders and delivery partners to develop a National Park Management Plan.

Other constituent authorities in the National Park, along with other government departments and public bodies, such as Natural England and the Environment Agency, have a responsibility to further the delivery of the National Parks purposes (the Protected Landscapes Duty). In return, the Peak District National Park Authority has a responsibility to engage with these bodies in developing the Management Plan.

These ‘relevant authorities’ – the local and combined authorities and other public bodies - are one of large land owners in the Peak District who contribute to delivering the National Park purposes. Others include environmental NGOs (non-governmental organisations) such as Wildlife Trusts and the Woodland Trust, as well as private estates. The below map shows some these major land owners, which account for about 40% of the Peak District’s total area. The other 60% is likely to be owned by private individuals such as farms and businesses; there is little data about this land ownership, but it shows that as they own 60% of the land these smaller land owners are also important contributors to delivering the National Park purposes.
